chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
title: Roy as world's greatest trumpeter; Dizzy jamming at the Savoy again
summary: Collins repeats the Paul Whiteman poll story that took Eldridge's band to the Savoy opposite Erskine Hawkins, where only Dizzy would jam with Roy.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: So during that time you had some great trumpet players, and of course Roy at that time was considered the president, as I stated before. Paul Whiteman was writing for (or something) the Saturday Evening Post Company, used to have this jazz poll. And he gave Roy the title of the king of the trumpet players, the world's greatest trumpet player. So on the strength of that we came back to New York from Chicago, and played at the Savoy, opposite as I -- I know I'm repeating myself but opposite Erskine Hawkins and the alternate band with Erskine Hawkins was -- oh, they had a little band. This was a rocking little band, the Savoy. Oh, what was the name of that band. Oh, that was a good little band. I forget.

But when we got through with them, though, we kind of demolished them, you know. But any way, Roy was riding the crest then and as I told you before the only one who would come up and play opposite Roy, jam with him really, was really

Dizzy Gillespie. But he was an innovator also. You see these things, you can't get away from. They are individualists. They are forever young, they have young ideas. They never stop, you know. Dizzy is just a great mind, you know, he's a very good piano player, you know, and his chordal sense -- oh, he's just tremendous. And he's always seeking. And so am I. You know, I've got to seek.
